parole.significato: county (a first-level country division in Denmark from 1662–2007)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German ambt, ambt, ambacht, from Proto-Germanic *ambahtiją, cognate with German Amt (“office”), Old Norse embætti. Doublet of embede (see more there).
From Middle Low German armōt, from Proto-Germanic *armōdiją, cognate with German Armut, Dutch armoede, Old Norse armœða. Derived from the adjective *armaz (“poor”).
From Middle Low German art, from Old Saxon *ard, from Proto-Germanic *ardiz, cognate with German Art.
From Middle Low German baten, batten, from Proto-Germanic *batāną (“to improve”), cognate with Dutch baten (“to avail”). Doublet of både.

From Middle Low German bedrṏven, drṏven, from Proto-Germanic *drōbijaną (“to trouble”), cognate with German trüben, Dutch droeven, Gothic 𐌳𐍂𐍉𐌱𐌾𐌰𐌽 (drōbjan) (Swedish bedröva is also from Low German). Derived from the adjective *drōbuz (“troubled”).
Borrowed from Middle Low German beginnen (“to begin”), from Proto-Germanic *biginnaną, cognate with German beginnen, English begin. Displaced native Danish børje (“to begin, start”).

parole.significato: to have a certain effect or influence on someone's feelings;
parole.testo: From Middle Low German bekomen, from Old Saxon bikuman, from Proto-Germanic *bikwemaną. Equivalent to be- + komme.

By surface analysis, be- + røve. From Middle Low German beroven, from Proto-Germanic *biraubōną. Cognate of Swedish beröva and Norwegian Bokmål berøve, Gothic 𐌱𐌹𐍂𐌰𐌿𐌱𐍉𐌽 (biraubōn), Dutch beroven, English bereave.
Equivalent to be- + sidde, literally “sit on”. From Middle Low German besitten, from Proto-Germanic *bisitjaną.

Equivalent to be- + stå (“to stand”). From Middle Low German bestân, from Proto-Germanic *bistandaną, *bistāną (“to stand by”), cognate with English bestand, German bestehen, Gothic 𐌱𐌹𐍃𐍄𐌰𐌽𐌳𐌰𐌽 (bistandan).
Borrowed from Middle Low German bī, from Proto-Germanic *bi (“near, around”). Related to English by and German bei.

parole.significato: to become (go from one state into another, with a predicative or the preposition til (“to”); the latter is preferred wi…
parole.testo: From Middle Low German bliven, from Old Saxon bilīƀan, from Proto-Germanic *bilībaną, cognate with German bleiben (“to remain”). In the sense “to become", it replaced native vorde.
From Middle Low German blōt (“bare”), from Proto-Germanic *blautaz (“void, emaciated, soft”), cognate with German bloß (“bare”) and Danish blød (“soft”).
From Middle Low German blōten, derived from blōt (“bare”), from Old Saxon *blōt, from Proto-Germanic *blautaz. See also Danish blot, and in a similar sense German entblößen.
From Middle Low German blöde, from Old Saxon blōthi, from Proto-Germanic *blauþuz. Related to etymology 1. Compare German blöd (“stupid, idiotic; slow”).
Borrowed from Middle Low German bōm (“tree”), from Proto-Germanic *baumaz, *bagmaz, compare German Baum and English beam.
From Middle Low German borde, from Proto-Germanic *burdô (“rim, edging”), cognate with German Borte. Probably related to *burdą (“board”).

parole.significato: board (a flat, long piece of wood, used as a material for building)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German bret, from Proto-Germanic *bredą, a byform of *burdą (“board”). Cognate with German Brett, Old English bred. Swedish bräde is also borrowed from Low German.

From Middle Low German bröke, from Proto-Germanic *brukiz (“breach”). The mathematical sense is a calque of Latin fractio. Cognate with German Bruch, Dutch breuk, English breach. Compare Swedish bråk, which is also borrowed from Low German.

parole.significato: to make unpleasant noise (often of rumbling, like from a car or machinery, or thunder)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German bulderen. Possibly Derived from Proto-Germanic *bellaną (“to roar”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰel-. Arguably onomatopoeic.
From Middle Low German bǖten, a verb derived from the former noun. Perhaps partially from Proto-Germanic *biūtijaną, a compound of *bi- and *ūtijaną (cf. Old Norse ýta, Danish yde).
From Middle Low German bate, from Proto-Germanic *batô (“improvement”), cognate with Dutch baat (“profit”) and Icelandic bati (“recovery”).
From Middle Low German baten, batten, from Proto-Germanic *batāną (“to improve”), cognate with Dutch baten (“to avail”). Doublet of batte.

From Middle Low German doch, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *þauh. Replaced native to, from Old Danish tho, from Old Norse þó. The word survived in Jutlandic dialects well into the 1950s as a discourse marker. Cf. also enddog.
From Middle Low German dracht (“what is carried”), from Proto-Germanic *drahtuz. Cognate with dræt and drage.

From Middle Low German drachtich, drechtich, from dracht, from Old Saxon *draht, from Proto-Germanic *drahtuz + the suffix -ig. Cognate with Dutch drachtig, German Low German drachtig, German trächtig, Norwegian Bokmål drektig, Norwegian Nynorsk drektig, Swedish dräktig.

parole.significato: tablecloth (a cloth used to cover and protect a table, especially for a dining table)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German dūk, dōk, from Proto-Germanic *dōkaz, cognate with German Tuch, Dutch doek (Old Norse dúkr is also borrowed from Low German).

parole.significato: a strong, unpleasant and nauseating odor
parole.testo: From Middle Low German dunst, from Old Saxon *dunst, from Proto-Germanic *dunstą.

parole.significato: to restrain oneself, to help oneself
parole.testo: Uncertain, possibly from Middle Low German dōgen (“to suffer, endure”), from Proto-Germanic *daugijaną, cognate with Dutch dogen (dialect).
From Middle Low German dempen, ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *dampaz.

Borrowed from Middle Low German ēgentlik (“actual”), related to Swedish egentlig, German eigentlich, Dutch eigenlijk. Derived from the adjective Middle Low German ēgen (“own”), from Proto-Germanic *aiganaz, cf. Danish egen, German eigen, English own.
From Middle Low German vāre (“danger, persecution, fear”), from Old Saxon fāra, from Proto-Germanic *fērō (“danger”), cognate with English fear, German Gefahr.

From earlier farge, from Middle Low German varwe, verwe, from *Old Saxon farwi, *farawi (“colour”), from Proto-Germanic *farwō, from Proto-Indo-European *per-, *perḱ- (“motley, coloured”). Cognate with Old High German farawa (“color”) (German Farbe), Old High German faro (“colored”), Latin pulcher (
From Middle Low German flink (“bright, shining, quick”). Perhaps ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *flakurōną (“to flutter, beat repeatedly”). Cognate to Plautdietsch flinkj (“quick”).

From Middle Low German vlī(g)en (“to stack, sort out”), cognate with Dutch vlijen (“to place”), from Proto-Germanic *flīhan, of unknown ultimate origin; possibly related to the root of *flaihijan (“to be sly, to flatter”), though the semantic gap is wide.

parole.significato: to make very afraid or shocked; to startle or shake violently
parole.testo: From Middle Low German vorveren, from vare (“danger, fear”), from Old Saxon *fāra, fār, from Proto-Germanic *fērō (“danger”). Compare Swedish förfära.
From Middle Low German vorlaten, from Proto-Germanic *fralētaną. Equivalent to for- + lade.
From Middle Low German vorlīden (“to pass”), derived from līden (“to go, suffer”), from Proto-Germanic *līþaną (hence Danish lide). A similar derivation in Old English forlīþan (“to shipwreck”).

parole.significato: to be shipwrecked (of a person at sea)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German vorliesen (“to lose”), from Proto-Germanic *fraleusaną, cognate with German verlieren, Dutch verliezen, English forlese (obsolete), Gothic 𐍆𐍂𐌰𐌻𐌹𐌿𐍃𐌰𐌽 (fraliusan).

parole.significato: to be capable, be able to
parole.testo: From Old Danish formughe, formue, from Middle Low German vormogen, from vor- + mogen (“may”), compare German vermögen. Doublet of formue (“fortune”). The second part of the verb is a cognate of Danish måtte (“can, must”), from Proto-Germanic *maganą.

From Middle Low German vrācht, vrēcht, a compound of Old Saxon far- and ēcht (“property”), from Proto-Germanic *aihtiz (“property”), cognate with Danish æt. German Fracht and Dutch vracht are also borrowed from Low German, and English freight and French fret (hence Spanish flete) are borrowed from M

parole.significato: foreign, alien (belonging to a different culture)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German vremede, from Proto-Germanic *framaþiz, cognate with Swedish främmande, German fremd.
Borrowed from Middle Low German vrō (“happy”), from Proto-Germanic *frawaz (“energetic”), cognate with German froh, Old Norse frár (“swift”).

parole.significato: pious, devout (religious in a serious way)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German vrome, from Proto-Germanic *frumô, related to German fromm, Dutch vroom (“pious”). In Old Saxon and Old High German, it is a noun meaning "use, benefit", but later it is used as an adjective.
From Middle Low German vruchte, from Proto-Germanic *furhtō, cognate with German Furcht. Related to the verb frygte (“to fear”).
From Middle Low German vruchten, from Proto-Germanic *furhtijaną, cognate with German fürchten.
From Middle Low German velge, from Proto-Germanic *felgō.
From Middle Low German vȫgen, from Proto-Germanic *fōgijaną, cognate with English fay, German fügen.
From Middle Low German gemene (“common”), from Proto-Germanic *gamainiz. Cognate with English mean and German gemein.
From Middle Low German gicht, a cognate of German Gicht, from Proto-Germanic *jihtiz.
From Middle Low German grus, ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *greutą (“grit”).

parole.significato: a badger (in particular the European badger, Meles meles)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German grevink (and grevel), derived from the verb graven (“to dig”), from Proto-Germanic *grabaną (Danish grave). The word has replaced older taks, from Proto-Germanic *þahsuz.

parole.significato: Used with a verb, indicating a movement towards or to something.
parole.testo: From Middle Low German hen, ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *hiz (“here”). Related to Swedish hän, English hence, and German hin.

From Middle Low German hengest, hengst, hingest, hingst, from Proto-Germanic *hangistaz, cognate with German Hengst. The Scandinavian word for “horse”, e.g. Danish hest, comes from a Verner alternation variant, *hanhistaz.

From Old Danish hurædan, where -dan is from Middle Low German wōdān, a compound of 1. wō (“how”) from Proto-Germanic *hwō, and 2. dān (“done”), past participle of dōn (“to do”), from Proto-Germanic *dōną. Compare Danish sådan (“so”), ligedan (“in the same way”). In Medieval Scandinavian, the first p

parole.significato: be hypocritical, to feign (e.g. piety, goodwill)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German hüchelen. It is probably derived from Proto-Germanic *hiwją (“shape, appearance”), cf. Gothic 𐌷𐌹𐍅𐌹 (hiwi) and English hue. The bible of Luther played a central role in propagating this word in Germany (German heucheln) and Scandinavia (Norwegian Bokmål hykle, Swedish hyckla).
From Middle Low German hǖpich, cognate with German häufig. Derived from the verb hūpe / Haufen (“heap”), from Proto-Germanic *hūpō. Related to *haupaz (English heap and, via Low German, Danish hob).

parole.significato: to fence (to sell stolen goods as a middleman)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German hēlen, from Proto-Germanic *helaną (“to hide, conceal”), cognate with German hehlen (“to fence”) and Dutch helen (“to fence”).
From Middle Low German hȫvelen, which has also been borrowed to Swedish hyvla. Derived from the noun hȫvel (“hill”), from Proto-Germanic *hubilaz, cognate with German Hübel (dialect), Dutch heuvel.

parole.significato: internal, inner (being inside something else, especially the body)
parole.testo: From Old Danish indwortes, indwærtes, borrowed from Middle Low German inwordes, inwerdes, a compound of in (“in”) + -werdes (“-ward”), compare Swedish invärtes, German einwärts, English inwards. The suffix derives from Proto-Germanic *wardaz (“turned”), cognate with German -wärts (borrowed to Danish
From Middle Low German klūteren, from Old Saxon *klōt, from Proto-Germanic *klautaz (“lump, block, knob”).

From Middle Low German knōp (“knot”), probably via Old Saxon from a variant of Proto-Germanic *knappô (“knob, lump”), one of several kn- words related to *knuttô (“knot”). Compare Dutch knoop and Swedish knop.

From Middle Low German krūsen, from krūs (“frizzy”), from Proto-Germanic *kruzlǭ (“bent or crooked object, curl”), possibly from Pre-Germanic *grus-, contracted from Proto-Indo-European *gurus- (“twist, curl”), same source as Persian گرس (gors, “braid of hair”).
From Old Danish krympæ, from Middle Low German krumpen, from Proto-Germanic *krimpaną

Borrowed from Middle Low German kreft, krevet (“crayfish, cancer”), from Proto-Germanic *krabitaz. Cognates include Swedish kräfta (“crayfish, cancer”) (also from Low German), German Krebs (“crayfish, cancer”) and Dutch kreeft (“crayfish”). The Danish word krebs (“crayfish”) is a German loan. The tr
From Middle Low German krullen, from Proto-Germanic *kruzlǭ, from Pre-Germanic *grus-, contracted from Proto-Indo-European *gurus- (“twist, curl”), same source as Persian گرس (gors, “braid of hair”).

From Middle Low German kunst, from Proto-Germanic *kunstiz (“knowledge, ability”), derived from the verb *kunnaną (“to know”). Cognate with German Kunst and Dutch kunst. Swedish konst was also borrowed from Low German.
Probably from Middle Low German keve, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *kebutaz. Doublet of kæft.

parole.significato: to hand, pass (in a careless manner)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German langen (“to reach for”), from Proto-Germanic *langōną, cognate with German langen, English long, Old Norse langa.
From Middle Low German lōve, from Proto-Germanic *galaubô, cognate with German Glaube.

From Old Danish lyktæ, borrowed from Middle Low German lūchte, from Proto-Germanic *liuhtijô, cognate with German Leuchte. Derived from Proto-Germanic *leuhtą (“light”), cf. English light and German Licht.

From Middle Low German lēren, from Proto-Germanic *laizijaną, cognate with German lehren (“teach”), Dutch leren, and Gothic 𐌻𐌰𐌹𐍃𐌾𐌰𐌽 (laisjan). Late Old Norse læra, Norwegian lære, and Swedish lära are also borrowed from Low German. For sense development from "teach" → "learn", compare Russian учи́ть

parole.significato: teachings, doctrine, theory (a coherent system of thoughts or ideas in science or religion)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German lēre, from Proto-Germanic *laizō (“teaching”), cognate with English lore, German Lehre, Dutch leer, and Gothic 𐌻𐌰𐌹𐍃𐍉 (laisō). Norwegian lære and Swedish lära are also borrowed from Low German.
From Middle Low German macht, from Proto-Germanic *mahtiz, derived from the verb from *maganą (“to be able”). Cognate with English might and German Macht. The Old Norse form was máttr (from *mahtuz).
From Middle Low German manen (“to remind”), from Old Saxon manōn, from Proto-Germanic *manōną, cognate with German mahnen.

parole.significato: to mean (to have a certain meaning in mind)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German meinen, mēnen (“to mean”), from Proto-Germanic *mainijaną, cognate with English mean, Dutch menen, German meinen (Icelandic meina and Swedish mena are also borrowed from Low German).
From Middle Low German middel, from Old Saxon middil, from Proto-Germanic *midlą. The noun is derived from the adjective.
From Middle Low German mos, from Proto-Germanic *mōsą (“mush, porridge”).

From Middle Low German olt, old, from Proto-Germanic *aldaz. Cognate with English old, Dutch oud, and German alt. The adjective exists in the Scandinavian languages only in the comparative and superlative, cf. ældre, ældst.

parole.significato: rebellion, revolt, insurrection, rising, uprising (protest against a leadership)
parole.testo: Formally a verbal noun of oprøre (“to shock”). Borrowed from Middle Low German uprōr, cognate with German Aufruhr m and Dutch oproer (whence English uproar). The word replaced an older, related noun with a similar meaning: Proto-Germanic *hrōzō, cf. Old Saxon hrōra, Old High German hruora, German Ru
From Middle Low German ōst (“east”), from Proto-Germanic *austrą. Cognate of Danish øster, Danish øst.

parole.significato: a blemish or rash resulting from smallpox, pockmarks, also similar conditions from syphilis, etc.
parole.testo: From Middle Low German pocke (“boil, abscess”), from Proto-Germanic *pukkaz, *pukkǭ (“pock; swelling”), cognate with English pock, pox, German Pocke. Maybe kopper (“smallpox”) is a euphemistic refashioning of this word.

parole.significato: prick (the feeling of being pierced or punctured by an object with a fine point, the action of pricking)
parole.testo: Formed from the verb prikke (“to poke lightly”), from Middle Low German pricke (“a prick”), pricken (“to prick”), from Old Saxon *prikkian, from Proto-Germanic *prikjaną.
From Middle Low German redden, from Proto-Germanic *hradjaną. Cognate with German retten.
From Middle Low German rēde, Middle Low German: gerēde, from Old Saxon *girēdi, from Proto-Germanic *raidijaz, *garaidijaz, cognate with English ready, Norwegian grei, Icelandic reiður, Swedish redo.

From Middle Low German rekenen, from Proto-Germanic *rekanōną. Cognate with English reckon, German rechnen, and Dutch rekenen. Icelandic reikna, Norwegian Nynorsk rekna, and Swedish räkna are also borrowed from Low German.
From Middle Low German renne, from Proto-Germanic *rinnǭ, cognate with German Rinne (“groove”), Gothic 𐍂𐌹𐌽𐌽𐍉 (rinnō, “brook”). Derived from the verb *rinnaną (“to run”).
From Middle Low German ribbe, rebbe (“rib, strip”), from Proto-Germanic *ribją, cognate with German Rippe, English rib, Old Norse rif (“reef”). Doublet of rev (“reef”).

From Middle Low German ribben (“to tear”), from Proto-Germanic *rippōną, *ribōną (“to tear off”), cognate with Dutch rippen, Faroese ripa, Norwegian ripe. An intensive of Proto-Germanic *rīfaną (“to tear”).

From Middle Low German ringe, from Old Saxon (gi)ringi (“light”), from Proto-Germanic *ga- + *reng-ja, of uncertain origin, but possibly from Proto-Indo-European *wrengʷʰ- (“to squeeze, wring”) and cognate with Proto-Germanic *wringaną (“to squeeze, wring”), Ancient Greek ῥίμφα (rhímpha, “fast, quic
From Middle Low German rotte, from Proto-Germanic *rattaz.

From Middle Low German rōkelōs, cognate with German ruchlos, English reckless, Dutch roekeloos. Derived from the noun Proto-Germanic *rōkō, hence Middle Low German rōke, Old High German ruohha. Possibly, this noun may go back to Proto-Indo-European *h₂roh₁g-eh₂-, cf. Ancient Greek ἀρωγή (arōgḗ, “hel

Borrwoed from Middle Low German schelen, from Proto-Germanic *skilhijaną (“to squint”), cf. also German schielen. Derived from the adjective Proto-Germanic *skelhaz, *skelgaz (“wry, oblique”), cf. Old Norse skjalgr (“squinty”), German scheel (“squinty”).

From Middle Low German (ge)schutte, from Proto-Germanic *gaskutją. Cognate with German Geschütz (“gun”), Dutch geschut (“artillery”). A collective from the noun *skutiz (“shot”), which is a verbal noun from *skeutaną. The modern Danish form is influenced by the Standard German cognate.
From Middle Low German schōnen, from Proto-Germanic *skaunijaną, derived from *skauniz (“beautiful”). Cognate with German schonen.
From Middle Low German schenken, from Proto-Germanic *skankijaną (“to tilt, pour”), cognate with German schenken, Old Norse skekkja (“to skew”).

From Middle Low German schȫke, from Proto-Germanic *skōkijō, cognate with Dutch scheuk (Swedish sköka and Old Norse skœkja are also borrowed from Low German). Perhaps related to the verb *skakaną (“to shake”).
From Middle Low German schorte (“armour”), from Proto-Germanic *skurtijǭ, cognate with English shirt, German Schürze (partly from Low German), Old Norse skyrta. Doublet of skjorte.
From Middle Low German slachten, from Proto-Germanic *slahaną, whence slå (“strike”).
From Middle Low German slap, from Proto-Germanic *slap-, perhaps ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)leh₂b- (“to be weak, limp, languid”), see also Latin labō (“fluctuate, waver”).
From Middle Low German slim, from Proto-Germanic *slimbaz. Compare German schlimm.
From Middle Low German slīpen, from Proto-Germanic *slīpaną. Cognate with German schleifen (“to whet”). Norwegian slipe and Swedish slipa.
Borrowed from Middle Low German slik, slīk, derived from the verb slīken (“to slide”), from Proto-Germanic *slīkaną. Cf. also Dutch slijk (“mud”) and German Schlick (“silt”).

From Middle Low German slot (“bolt, lock, castle”), from Proto-Germanic *slutą, related to the verb *sleutaną (“to lock”); cognate with Dutch slot (“lock, castle”) and German Schloss (“lock, castle”), and comparable to Swedish slott (“castle, palace; manor, château”).
From Middle Low German slūken, slucken, from Proto-Germanic *slūkōną, *slukkōną. Cognate with German schlucken and Dutch slokken.

From Middle Low German slecht (“family, lineage”), related to German Geschlecht (“gender, lineage”) and Dutch geslacht (“gender, lineage”). Derived from Proto-Germanic *slahtō, which belongs to the verb Proto-Germanic *slahaną.
From Middle Low German smaken, from Proto-Germanic *smakōną, *smakkōną, *smakkijaną (“to taste”). Cognate with German schmecken and English smake, smack.
From Middle Low German smerten, from Proto-Germanic *smertaną.
From Middle Low German smitten (“to stain”), from Proto-Germanic *smittōną.

From Middle Low German sniddeker, derived from the verb sniddeken, snidken (“to carve”), a variant of the verb snīden (“to cut”), from Proto-Germanic *snīþaną. Norwegian snekker and Swedish snickare are also borrowed from Low German.
From Middle Low German spit, from Old Saxon *spit, from Proto-Germanic *spituz (“stick, rod”).

From Old Danish sprethæ, from Middle Low German sprēden, spreiden, from Proto-Germanic *spraidijaną (“to spread”). Cognate with English spread and German spreiten. Due to the absence of this word in Old Icelandic, the Danish word as well as Norwegian Bokmål spre, Norwegian Nynorsk spreie and Swedish

parole.significato: blubber (of a whale or a seal)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German spek, from Proto-Germanic *spiką, cognate with German Speck (“bacon”), English speck (“fat”), Old Norse spik. The geminate consonant of Danish spæk(k-), Norwegian spekk and Swedish späck points to a Low German origin (the Old Norse form would have resulted in Danish *

From Middle Low German spȫken, from Old Saxon *spōk, from Proto-Germanic *spōk (“wizardry, witchcraft”). cognate with Dutch spoken (“to haunt”), English spook (from Dutch), German spuken (from Low German). Derived from the noun spōk (Danish spøg).

parole.significato: voice (sound uttered by the mouth, especially that uttered by human beings in speech or song)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German stemme, stemne, stimme, from Proto-Germanic *stamnijō (“voice, sound”). Cognate of English steven and German Stimme. The meaning "vote" is influenced by modern German Stimme. The Norse word røst is still in use.
From Middle Low German stoppen, from Proto-Germanic *stuppōną, cognate with German stopfen and the former verb.
From Middle Low German stripe, from Proto-Germanic *stripan, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *streyg- (“to rub, stroke”).

parole.significato: to stow, pack (place things or people in a limited space with little room between them)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German stūwen, stōwen, from Proto-Germanic *stōjaną (“to stow”), cognate with German stauen, German stauen, Dutch stuwen, Gothic 𐍃𐍄𐍉𐌾𐌰𐌽 (stōjan, “to judge”). Derived from the noun *stōō (“place, stowage”).
Partly derived directly from the verb styre and partly a loan from Middle Low German stǖr, from Proto-Germanic *stiuriją. Doublet of styre.

From Middle Low German stof, from Old Saxon *stiof, from Proto-Germanic *stubą, *stuba, derived from the verb *steubaną (“to smoke”). Swedish stoft is also borrowed from Low German. The Danish form has taken over the vowel from the verb støve.

From Middle Low German swichten (“to yield”), cognate with Dutch zwichten (“to yield”), Middle High German swiften (“to silence”), and German beschwichtigen (“to conciliate”) (with Low German -cht-). These verbs are derived from the adjective Proto-Germanic *swiftaz (“moving”) (whence English swift)

parole.significato: brother-in-law (the brother of one's spouse, husband of one's sibling or husband of one's spouse's sibling)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German swāger, from Proto-Germanic *swēgraz (“husband's brother”), cognate with German Schwager, Dutch zwager. Swedish svåger is also borrowed from Low German. The word goes back to Proto-Indo-European *swēḱurós (“husband's brother”), related to *swéḱuros (“father-in-law”) (German Sc
From Middle Low German swavel, from Old Saxon sweval, from Proto-Germanic *sweblaz. Related to Latin sulfur.
From Middle Low German swēven, from Old Saxon *swivian, from Proto-Germanic *swibāną.
From Middle Low German sulte, from Old Saxon *sultia, from Proto-Germanic *sultijō (“salt water, brine”). Compare German Sülze and Dutch zult. Cognate with salt (“salt”).

From Old Danish tanckæ, from Middle Low German danke, from Old Saxon thanc, from Proto-Germanic *þankaz (with the initial consonant of the related verb Danish tænke (“think”)). The Middle Low German word has also been borrowed to Swedish tanke, Norwegian tanke, and Icelandic þanki.

From Middle Low German telt, from Proto-Germanic *teldą. Cognate with German Zelt and Old Norse tjald (“tent”) (whence Norwegian Bokmål tjeld, Swedish tjäll, and Danish tjæld). English tilt and Swedish tält were also borrowed from Low German.
Borrowed from Middle Low German toge, toch, from Old Saxon *tugi, from Proto-Germanic *tugiz. Cognate with Dutch teug, German Zug, Old English tyge. The sense "train" is derived from German Zug.

From Middle Low German tucht, from Proto-Germanic *tuhtiz (“pulling”). Cognate with German Zucht (“discipline”) and Dutch tocht (“expedition”) (whence Danish togt). Late Old Norse tykt and Swedish tukt are also borrowed from Low German. The Germanic noun is derived from the verb *teuhaną (“to lead,
From Old Danish thwang, from Middle Low German dwank, from Proto-Germanic *þwanguz, *þwangiz, cognate with Swedish tvång n, English thong, German Zwang, Old Norse þvengr (“thong”). Doublet of tvinge.

parole.significato: to hesitate (to stop or pause respecting decision or action)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German tȫven, from Proto-Germanic *tōbijaną, cognate with Dutch toeven (“to linger”). Derived from the noun *tōbą (“hesitation”) (Icelandic tóf) and related to the verb *tabijaną (“to delay”) (Old Norse tefja).
From Middle Low German unhure, ungehure. Compare German Ungeheuer, = un- + geheuer (“pleasant”). The adjective has a cognate in Old Norse hýrr (“pleasant, friendly”), from Proto-Germanic *hiurijaz.
u- (“un-”) + lyst (“desire, lust”). From Middle Low German unlust, from Proto-Germanic *unlustuz (“listlessness”).

parole.significato: Inseparable verb prefix indicating removing something from the object, from, away from, off.
parole.testo: Partly a loan from Middle Low German ent-, unt-, from Proto-Germanic *andi- (cf. German ent-), and partly an abbreviation of Old Norse undan, from Proto-Germanic *undanē (“down under”).

parole.significato: to conceive (a child or an idea)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German untvangen, entvangen. Cf. German empfangen (“to receive, conceive”). The second part of this word is from Proto-Germanic *fanhaną (“to take, catch”).

und- (“away”) + være (“to be”). A remodelling of Middle Low German entberen, Middle Low German untberen, cf. German entbehren. The second part of this word is Proto-Germanic *beraną (“to carry, bear”). Swedish umbära was also borrowed from Low German.
From Middle Low German wacht, wachte, from Proto-Germanic *wahtwō, cognate with German Wacht. Norwegian vakt and Swedish vakt are also borrowed from Low German.

From Middle Low German wittich (“sensible, intelligent”), derived from the noun witte, wit, from Proto-Germanic *witją. Compare German witzig from Witz. The current sense from French spirituel (“witty”) via German witzig (“funny, humo(u)rous”).
From Middle Low German wachten, derived from the noun wacht, wachte (“guard”), from Proto-Germanic *wahtwō.
From vogte (“to guard”) + -er, or borrowed from Middle Low German wachter, derived from the noun wacht, wachte (“guard”), from Proto-Germanic *wahtwō. Compare German Wächter.
From Middle Low German wal, from Proto-Germanic *wallaz, *wallą, an early borrowing of Latin vallum; cognate with English wall, German Wall.

From Middle Danish waaghe, wogæ, wowæ, from Middle Low German wagen, from Proto-Germanic *wagōną. Cognate with German wagen, Dutch wagen, Old Norse vaga (“to waddle”) (late Old Norse voga and Swedish våga are also borrowed from Low German). Doublet of vugge.
From Middle Low German wāch m, wāge f, from Proto-Germanic *wēgaz, cognate with English waw (obsolete), Dutch waag f, Old Norse vágr (“sea; bay”). Doublet of våg.

From Old Danish wict, wæct, from Middle Low German wicht, from Proto-Germanic *wihtiz. The old Nordic form of the word is found in Old Danish wæt. Cognate with English weight, Latin vectis. Swedish vikt is also borrowed from Low German.
From Middle Low German wechter, wachter, derived from wacht (“watch”), from Proto-Germanic *wahtwō. Compare German Wächter. Norwegian vekter and Swedish väktare are also borrowed from Low German.
From Middle Low German wert (“host”), from Proto-Germanic *werduz, cognate with German Wirt, Dutch waard, Gothic 𐍅𐌰𐌹𐍂𐌳𐌿𐍃 (wairdus). Swedish värd is also borrowed from Low German.

Borrowed from Middle Low German ūteren (“challenge, declare, drive out, give away”), compare German äußern and English utter. Derived from Middle Low German ūtere (“outer”), Old High German ūzaro, Old English ūtera, an adjective formed to the adverb Proto-Germanic *ūt (“out”).

From Middle Low German orsake (“reason, cause”), related to German Ursache. It is a compound of or- + sake / ur- + Sache, from Proto-Germanic *uz- (“out”) and *sakō (“case”). From Middle Low German echt, whence also German echt (“lawful”). Originally a compound of 1. Middle Low German ē (“law, marriage”) (German Ehe (“marriage”)), from Proto-Germanic *aiwǭ, *aiwaz (“law”), and 2. German -haft, from Proto-Germanic *haftaz (“captured, afflicted”). parole.significato: to practise (with or without an object)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German ȫven, from Old Saxon ōvian, from Proto-Germanic *ōbijaną (“to do, practise”). Cognate with German üben.
